summary:
Zamfara State stands under two overlapping layers of criminal law. Nigeria's national framework, the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014, binds every person in the country including visitors; the UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex sex between men under secular law, and Human Rights Watch ('Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe', October 2016) documents that the Act reaches well beyond marriage, banning cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with 10 to 14 years' imprisonment. The same Human Rights Watch record shows police using the statute to justify torture and arbitrary arrest.

Zamfara is the jurisdiction where Nigeria's Sharia criminal-law wave began. Human Rights Watch (2004) records that Zamfara's governor was the first to act, introducing the Sharia Establishment Law on 27 October 1999, in force 27 January 2000; by 2002 twelve northern states had adopted some form of Sharia into their criminal legislation, and to date those twelve are the only states where Sharia courts hold jurisdiction to try criminal cases. A visitor in Zamfara is therefore subject to a religious criminal code that operates alongside, not instead of, the national Act.

Zamfara's own legal architecture is documented in the state's account of its adoption, set out by its then Attorney-General and Commissioner for Justice, Alh. Ahmed Bello Mahmud, at a JNI-sponsored seminar on 6 July 2000. The enabling legislation, the Sharia Courts (Administration of Justice and Certain Consequential Changes) Law 1999, was enacted under section 6 of the 1999 Constitution and established Sharia courts with criminal jurisdiction in Islamic law, enabling the codification of a Sharia Penal Code; the Grand Kadi took over court administration on 29 June 2000. The governor had appointed a committee in June 1999 mandated to study implementation, including the full scope of Islamic criminal law, and the resulting codification of offences and punishments produced the penal-code architecture that the Sharia courts of all twelve states apply, a framework Zamfara pioneered across the northern bloc.

For an LGBT+ visitor the practical consequence of that framework is capital risk. The UK Home Office assesses that Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions. The latest UK FCDO travel advice for Nigeria, reported by Sahara Reporters in August 2026, warns of attacks, blackmail and intimidation against LGBT+ travellers, up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states. Zamfara is one of those states.

Enforcement nationally takes the form of mass arrests at social venues rather than isolated prosecutions, and the pattern reaches the north. Men arrested in Bauchi in August 2007 were held for several years awaiting a trial that had dissolved by end-2011, and 76 people were arrested at a party in Gombe state in October 2023. The same tactic has been used in the south, with 100-plus party-goers arrested at a hotel in Asaba, Delta State, in June 2018 and 57 young men at Egbeda, Lagos, in August 2018, alongside the 'Warri 67' in Warri, Delta State, in August 2023.

Appearance alone is treated as grounds for police action. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that a 24-year-old man, Okafor, was stopped by Lagos police, struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and freed only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for 'looking gay'; those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law creating a climate of hostility. Trans Nigerians face lethal violence with official misgendering and subsequent impunity: the beaten body of the Abuja trans TikToker 'Abuja Area Mama', a 33-year-old transgender woman, was found on a highway in Abuja in August 2024, hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend, and police said preliminary investigations showed 'a man fully dressed in female clothing'. Six months later, in February 2025, The Dial reported that no suspects had been charged.

Two further exposures apply directly to a visitor's conduct. Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents 'kito' gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and other apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing, and Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians fear proposals to criminalise cross-dressing as a discrete offence.

Imprisonment raises placement questions that remain unresolved. Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye) pleaded guilty to four counts of Naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine; she served the term in Kirikiri maximum-security prison, Lagos, and was released on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison would hold 'the crossdresser', reflecting discretionary placement, and an October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that placing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

Care access is chilled by arrest and extortion risk. Many LGBTQ Nigerians fear seeking medical care or reporting crimes, and activists say the Same-Sex Marriage Prohibition Act hampers access to HIV prevention services and forces LGBTQ people and allies to abandon community health and education work.
tangentialFactors:
A decade-outcome assessment of the national statute exists. Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (August 2024), marking ten years of the SSMPA, finds that the 2014 law has fuelled violence, extortion and discrimination far beyond its scope and has effectively sanctioned abuse, with LGBTQ+ Nigerians reporting lost job prospects and increased attacks since it passed.

Venues and organisations that could serve as points of contact face closure and exposure. The House of Rainbow Metropolitan Church in Lagos cancelled conferences after members' names and addresses were published in four newspapers on 12 September 2008 and some were threatened, beaten and stoned.

Zamfara's pioneering role gives its arrangements a comparative significance beyond its own borders: eleven other northern states had adopted the application of Sharia by the end of 2000, and the codified offences and punishments produced in that period became the penal-code architecture applied by the Sharia courts of all twelve states.

outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory records a prosecution brought under the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act within Zamfara State specifically, nor a death sentence imposed on a same-sex conduct charge in Zamfara; the death penalty is sourced as available under state Zina provisions in all twelve northern states, not as having been imposed here.

Whether the September 2022 proposals to criminalise cross-dressing were enacted, and in what form, is not sourced and remains unresolved.

The status of the February 2025 finding that no suspects had been charged in the killing of 'Abuja Area Mama' has no later update in the inventory.

Rules governing the placement of transgender prisoners in Zamfara's own correctional facilities are not sourced; the only placement record concerns the Kirikiri facility in Lagos and a October 2024 panel finding on the Nigerian Correctional Service Act.

The current UK FCDO travel advice is sourced through a August 2026 press report of the advice rather than the primary advisory text.
